question: According to many experts, human genome research is the future of medicine. The market is expected to reach a value of hundreds of billions of dollars within a decade, providing new opportunities for medicine and biotechnology, and allowing a new generation of personalised medication to emerge, e.g. for cancer and rare illnesses.

However, the development of this medical technology comes not only with ethical concerns, but also with security risks. Security institutions are paying close attention to the activity of companies connected to the Chinese Government and military, such as BGI Group and MGI, which want to dominate this part of the industry.

In the meantime, reports from China suggest that companies are complicit in the mass surveillance of Chinese citizens, including as part of the Uyghur genocide. Security services warn that genetic databases can be used to attack people and ethnic groups based on their genetic profile, to genetically engineer countries’ own soldiers or to alter viruses.
The United States is already taking legislative action aimed at preventing the transfer of sensitive genetic data to countries such as China and Russia. 1.

Does the Commission share the concerns of the security services and experts who describe in detail how, under the guise of research and development, China is using this genetic data for purposes that are clearly at odds with the EU’s values, ethical standards and security interests?

Is the Commission aware of the revelations relating to the Chinese authorities’ keen interest in the genetic profiling of ethnic minorities in order to pursue a policy of control and surveillance against vulnerable groups, including ethnic minorities?
answer: The Commission is aware that genome research and use of genetic data could pose risks. The Commission Recommendation of 3 October 2023 (1) identified biotechnologies as one of ten critical technology areas for economic security and launched joint risk assessments with Member States in four critical technology areas, including biotechnologies, posing the most sensitive risk for European economic security.

In line with the Global Approach to Research and Innovation (R&I) (2), safeguarding measures are implemented in Horizon Europe, including under Article 22(5) of the Horizon Europe Regulation (3) which allows to restrict the participation of certain entities in specific calls in the Work Programmes, the ethics screening process (ensuring a focus on civil applications and that the highest ethical standards are abided by), and Article 40(4) relating to the right to object to transfers of ownership of results.

Specific restrictions have also been inserted in the current Work Programme 2023-2025 using Article 22(6) to exclude Chinese entities from participating in high-tech innovation and 5G- related actions.

Beyond Horizon Europe, and in full respect/ of academic freedom and institutional autonomy of R&I sector entities, the Commission is working to raise awareness on research security and encourage due diligence processes. In 2022, the toolkit on tackling foreign R&I interference (4) was published to help research performing organisations counter threats from foreign state-actors.

As a follow-up to the 2023 Economic Security Strategy (5), in January 2024, the Commission presented a proposal for a Council recommendation on enhancing research security 2024 (6). The Council adopted the recommendation on 23 May 2024.
